title: Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance in the Congenital Heart Disease Transition Clinic: Establishing the Adult Baseline for Lifelong Care—A Narrative Review
content: Advances in paediatric cardiology, surgery, intensive care and catheter interventions have enabled most children born with congenital heart disease (CHD) to reach adulthood. The transition from paediatric to adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) care remains a vulnerable period marked by risk of discontinuity, delayed recognition of residual lesions, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias, aortopathy and other late complications. Cardiovascular imaging is therefore essential at this juncture. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) provides comprehensive, radiation-free assessment of anatomy, ventricular volumes and function, blood ﬂow, regurgitation, shunts and myocardial tissue characteristics. Its role in the transition clinic is not to replace echocardiography or to serve as a universal screening tool, but to resolve clinically important questions that echocardiography cannot answer reliably and to establish a reproducible quantitative baseline for lifelong adult follow-up. CMR is particularly valuable after repair of tetralogy of Fallot, in systemic right ventricles after atrial switch, in Fontan circulation, coarctation of the aorta, pulmonary artery abnormalities, anomalous venous connections, and other complex postoperative anatomies. Findings directly inﬂuence surveillance intervals, risk stratiﬁcation, exercise and pregnancy counselling, referral for catheterisation, and the timing of surgical or transcatheter reintervention. Limitations include examination duration, claustrophobia, arrhythmia-related degradation, device artefacts, contrast considerations, limited availability, and the need for congenital imaging expertise. A strategically timed CMR examination during transition bridges paediatric surgical history with adult care. By deﬁning an accurate adult baseline and detecting clinically silent abnormalities, CMR supports continuity, individualised surveillance, shared decision-making and lifelong management. Its use should remain lesion-speciﬁc, question-driven and integrated within a multimodality transition pathway.
